expansion:
MRI is the correct "not advised" investigation because the lecture states this as a core rule when a metallic intraocular foreign body is suspected: “SLIDE 52 — If you suspect IOFB ★ CORE... DO NOT DO MRI SCAN IF A METALLIC IOFB IS SUSPECTED” (L25, slide 52). A mechanic hammering iron who feels something strike the eye, with a sealed entry wound in the cornea, is the classic setup for a retained metallic intraocular foreign body from a high-velocity metal fragment; the strong magnetic field of an MRI scanner can move or heat a ferromagnetic fragment lodged inside the globe, causing further mechanical damage to intraocular structures.

CT eye and orbit, option A, is explicitly recommended instead of MRI in this scenario: the same slide lists "CT SCAN — Determine the location and presence of a metallic IOFB [and] show the shape and integrity of the traumatized globe" (L25, slide 52), so it is an appropriate, advised investigation, not a contraindicated one.

Plain X-ray to the orbit, option B, is likewise listed as an appropriate investigation on the same slide — "Investigation may include: Plain film x-rays of the head" (L25, slide 52) — and plain films have long been used to screen for radio-opaque metallic foreign bodies, so it is advised rather than avoided.

B-scan ultrasound, option D, is also listed among the useful investigations on that slide ("Ultrasound may be useful", L25, slide 52), and the accompanying figures show a B-scan ultrasound image of an IOFB (L25, slide 53/54); it is generally used cautiously (avoiding pressure on an open globe) but is not the investigation the lecture singles out as prohibited — that designation is reserved for MRI alone.
objective: Recall that MRI is contraindicated when a metallic intraocular foreign body is suspected, unlike CT, plain X-ray or B-scan ultrasound
